Select a reference image $I_{\text{ref}}$ which has the closest averaged color value $(r_{\text{ref}}, g_{\text{ref}}, b_{\text{ref}}) \in \mathbb{R}^3$ to $(r_a, g_a, b_a)$ [S2].

The claim states that a reference image is selected based on having the closest averaged color value to the averaged color of all inputs. Source [S2] explicitly states: 'we calculate the averaged color of all inputs (ra , ga , ba ) ∈ R3 , select a reference image which has the closest value of (ra , ga , ba )'. This directly supports every fact in the claim.
supported
It addresses the limitation of prior methods that only correct exposure at training views by generalizing to images rendered at any novel viewpoint [S1].

The claim states that the method addresses the limitation of prior methods (which only correct exposure at training views) by generalizing to novel viewpoints. Source [S1] explicitly states: 'Unlike existing works [6, 17] that only correct the exposure at training views, our strategy can generalize to images rendered at any viewpoint.' This directly supports every part of the claim.
supported
*   **Sparse Training Data:** If the nearest neighbor is far away, the assumption of similar global lighting conditions may fail, leading to incorrect exposure correction [S1].

The claim states that if the nearest neighbor is far away, the assumption of similar global lighting conditions may fail. The evidence explicitly states that the method 'assume[s] that images taken at nearby locations share similar global lighting conditions' and corrects exposure by 'mimicking the exposure setting of the closest source view.' This implies that the validity of the correction relies on the proximity of the source view; if the nearest neighbor is not 'nearby' (i.e., far away), the underlying assumption of similar lighting conditions would not hold, leading to the failure described in the claim.
supported
Calculate the averaged color $(r_a, g_a, b_a) \in \mathbb{R}^3$ of all input images in the set $S$ [S2].

The claim states that the evidence supports calculating the averaged color $(r_a, g_a, b_a)$ of all input images in the set $S$. Source [S2] explicitly states in the notes: 'Calculate averaged color (ra, ga, ba) of all input images.' Furthermore, the passage confirms this by stating: 'we calculate the averaged color of all inputs (ra , ga , ba ) ∈ R3'. The notation and the action described in the claim match the evidence exactly.
supported
*   Neighbor count: 1 (nearest neighbor only) [S1].

The claim states that the neighbor count is 1 (nearest neighbor only). The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly mentions correcting exposure by 'mimicking the exposure setting of the closest source view' and refers to the 'nearest neighbouring view'. This confirms that the method relies on a single nearest neighbor.
supported
This is an initialization strategy to resolve the ambiguity between exposure and white balance, stabilizing optimization by guiding initial solutions to physically plausible ones [S2].

The claim accurately reflects the content of Source [S2]. The source explicitly states that the initialization strategy is used to 'workaround the scale ambiguity between exposure and white balance' and that it 'guides initial solutions to physically plausible solutions; thereby, the optimization process becomes more stable'. These points directly match the claim's description of resolving ambiguity and stabilizing optimization.
supported
Apply the exposure correction from $I_{\text{nn}}$ to the rendered radiance at $V_{\text{novel}}$ [S1].

The claim states that the exposure correction from the nearest neighbor ($I_{nn}$) is applied to the rendered radiance at the novel view ($V_{novel}$). The evidence explicitly states that the method 'correct the camera exposure at novel views by mimicking the exposure setting of the closest source view' and that this strategy 'generalize[s] to images rendered at any viewpoint.' This confirms that the correction derived from the nearest source view is indeed applied to the rendered images at novel viewpoints.
unsupported
Retrieve the exposure setting (or implicit exposure scaling factor) associated with $I_{\text{nn}}$ [S1].

The evidence describes a strategy to correct exposure by mimicking the exposure setting of the closest source view, but it does not mention or define a specific variable named '$I_{nn}$' or an 'implicit exposure scaling factor' associated with it.
supported

*   **Dynamic Exposure:** When exposure differences are significantly dynamic among neighborhood views, the method may still struggle if the nearest neighbor has a vastly different exposure setting, potentially causing the renderer to misinterpret exposure differences as high-frequency reflectance [S2].

The claim states that when exposure differences are significantly dynamic among neighborhood views, the method may struggle if the nearest neighbor has a vastly different exposure setting, causing the renderer to misinterpret exposure differences as high-frequency reflectance. Source [S2] explicitly states: 'We observe that when the exposure differences are significantly dynamic among neighborhood views, observed LDR intensity differences by exposure times are misunderstood as the cause of the high-frequency reflectance... of the scene'. This directly supports the core mechanism described in the claim.
supported

This acts as regularization.' This directly supports the claim.
supported

Fails when nearby views have significantly different exposure settings, as the nearest neighbor assumption breaks down and may cause the renderer to misinterpret exposure differences as high-frequency reflectance [S2].

The evidence in Source [S2] explicitly states that when 'exposure differences are significantly dynamic among neighborhood views,' the system misunderstands 'observed LDR intensity differences by exposure times' as 'high-frequency reflectance' of the scene. This matches the claim's assertion that the renderer may misinterpret exposure differences as high-frequency reflectance when nearby views have significantly different exposure settings.
supported
It addresses the issue where the overall scale of white balance becomes extremely small or large during training [S2].

The evidence explicitly states that with the previous representation, 'the overall scale of the white balance is trained extremely small or large.' It then describes the proposed method (calculating averaged colors, selecting a reference image, and fixing its white balance) as a solution that 'helps white balance be learned on the proper scale.' This directly supports the claim that the method addresses the issue of the white balance scale becoming extremely small or large.
supported
This strategy corrects inconsistent exposure across training views caused by the auto-exposure behavior of modern cameras in radiance-field optimization [S1].

The claim states that the strategy corrects inconsistent exposure across training views caused by auto-exposure behavior. The evidence explicitly states: 'our method to address inconsistent exposure across training views caused by the auto-exposure behavior of modern cameras' and describes the strategy as 'correct the camera exposure at novel views by mimicking the exposure setting of the closest source view.' The evidence confirms both the problem (inconsistent exposure due to auto-exposure) and the nature of the strategy described in the claim.
supported
The strategy was introduced in the context of Image-Based Gaussian Splatting (IBGS) to address photometric inconsistencies arising from auto-exposure in modern cameras [S1].

The evidence explicitly states that the method addresses 'inconsistent exposure across training views caused by the auto-exposure behavior of modern cameras' and introduces an 'exposure correction strategy' within an 'image-based Gaussian Splatting pipeline'. The claim accurately reflects these points.
supported
*   **Limitations:** Relies on the assumption of similar lighting between nearby views [S1].

The claim states that the method relies on the assumption of similar lighting between nearby views. The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly states: 'we assume that images taken at nearby locations share similar global lighting conditions, and thus correct the camera exposure at novel views by mimicking the exposure setting of the closest source view.' This directly supports the claim.
